title: Inherent interpretability provides inherent value in quantum machine learning
abstract: The field of quantum machine learning (QML) evolved to value models believed to most directly rival those providing utility in classical ML, namely large-scale neural networks. Although more recently, classical ML has been learning a hard lesson with respect to deploying un-interpretable neural networks in the wild: model interpretability matters for domain-adapted co-design and human adoption. We adopt this larger ML perspective to argue that quantum ML model value can be found through the characterization of its inherent interpretability offerings -- i.e. its mathematical structure that contributes meaningfully to desired model behavior for the specific ML task. To support our perspective, we provide a motivating example of a characterization with quantum Fourier models and random Fourier features (RFF) as approaches to approximate Gaussian process (GP) kernels for uncertainty quantification tasks in ML. The top-down and bottom-up complementarity of the two mathematical constructions reveals that quantum Fourier models offer different tools than RFFs for principled GP kernel design and interpretable discovery for uncertainty quantification with real-world data. To showcase the rich variety of inductive biases enabled by quantum information tools, we review examples from the QML literature -- including symmetry, metric geometry, and topology -- that can be used to design inherently interpretable ML models for specific tasks. We hope this framing encourages the QML community to value the inherent components and mechanisms of quantum models separately from task performance, as inherent interpretability might be the reason that a quantum model, and potentially a quantum computer, gets used in practice for ML.
summary: This paper argues that the true value of Quantum Machine Learning lies in its inherent mathematical structure—its interpretability—rather than just its performance relative to classical methods. It demonstrates this by comparing how quantum Fourier models and Random Fourier Features can both approximate GP kernels, showing that quantum tools offer unique mechanisms for principled model design. This reframes QML research to value the underlying physical or mathematical components of quantum circuits.
main_problem: The field of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) needs a value proposition beyond merely matching classical ML performance, especially given that model interpretability is crucial for real-world deployment.
main_result: The value of QML models should be characterized by their inherent mathematical structure and interpretability offerings, rather than solely by task performance metrics.
method: The authors compare quantum Fourier models against Random Fourier Features (RFF) in the context of designing interpretable Gaussian Process (GP) kernels for uncertainty quantification.
model_or_system: The work analyzes parameterized quantum circuits (QNNs) and uses Bayesian linear regression within a GP framework. It compares feature mapping techniques derived from classical spectral distributions (RFF) versus those arising naturally from quantum information tools (Quantum Fourier Models).
key_observables: Model interpretability, uncertainty quantification ($\sigma^2_{	ext{pred}}$), and the ability to encode domain-specific inductive biases.
important_parameters: The spectral distribution $p(\omega_z)$ controlling RFFs; the Hamiltonian families $\{H^{(l)}_j\}$ used in quantum feature mapping.
main_assumptions: The argument assumes that demonstrating inherent interpretability benefits justifies the use of potentially resource-intensive quantum computation for ML tasks.
figures_summary: Figure 1 visually contrasts the bottom-up kernel design approach using Hamiltonian families (Quantum Fourier Models) against the top-down spectral distribution choice in RFFs.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for interpretability in QML, provides a detailed mathematical comparison between Quantum Fourier Models and RFFs via GP kernels, and concludes with a review of various quantum information tools (symmetry, topology) that enable inherently interpretable model design.
why_interesting: It bridges advanced topics like algebraic topology and group theory (used to constrain models) directly into the practical methodology of machine learning, offering theoretical frameworks for building physically motivated quantum algorithms.
